title: The gnostic's virtues and conduct
english: Practical ascetics will understand practical words, and gnostics will see gnostic things.
A practical ascetic is one who has acquired only the passionate part of the soul as free from passion.
A gnostic is one who serves as salt for the impure, and as light for the pure.

The knowledge that comes to us from outside tries to point out material things through words, but the knowledge that arises within by God's grace presents the things themselves to the mind by direct vision. The mind looks at these things and receives their principles. Error is opposed to the former kind of knowledge, but anger and wrath and the things that follow these are opposed to the latter.

All the virtues make a road for the gnostic, but above all, freedom from anger. For the one who has grasped spiritual knowledge and is easily moved to anger is like a man piercing his own eyes with an iron pin.

Let the gnostic be on guard in his accommodations, lest accommodation secretly become a fixed habit in him. And let him strive always to practice all the virtues equally, so that they follow one another in him, because the mind is naturally betrayed by the virtue that is lacking.
It is shameful for a gnostic to go to court, whether he has been wronged or has wronged another: if he has been wronged, because he did not endure it; if he has wronged another, because he did wrong.
Spiritual knowledge, when it is guarded, teaches the one who shares in it how he may be preserved and advance to greater things.
It is right to discuss correct conduct with monks and people in the world and to clarify in part the teachings of natural and theological doctrine, without which no one will see the Lord.
Learn the principles and laws of times, ways of life, and occupations, so that you may readily say what is beneficial to each person.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Evagrius opens the treatise by defining the practical ascetic and the gnostic, then gives counsels on the virtues, especially freedom from anger, and on the gnostic's speech and conduct.
